WHAT IT COSTS · EXAMPLE 1
Health Net: a $40M lesson
$40M
$12M paid, plus about $28.5M of required changes over six years
California Attorney General, October 2025. Health Net, a Centene company, was accused of using inaccurate mental-health and medical provider directories.
WHAT THE SETTLEMENT REQUIRES
Check contact details and new-patient status using claims, contracts, utilization and public data
Automatically remove duplicate, unlicensed or deceased entries
Label providers who offer only telehealth
Show the date each entry was last updated
Our take: the fix regulators asked for is close to what we propose. We add an order for the calls, by dollars at risk, and an evidence log.
Sources: California Attorney General release; Becker’s Payer Issues. A settlement resolves allegations; it is not a court finding.

82%
of its providers called in a 2023 New York AG review were not available for an appointment
  • City employees and the American Psychiatric Association sued in January 2026

THE PLAN’S EXPOSURE · SUMMARY
Four ways a wrong directory hits the plan
1. Member lawsuits
Class actions claim deception, false advertising, fraud and unjust enrichment. Some have survived dismissal.
2. State enforcement
Health Net: $12M paid plus about $28.5M of required changes.
3. Federal rules
Verify every 90 days, remove what cannot be verified, correct within 2 business days. Excise tax of up to $100 a day per affected person; how often it is enforced is unconfirmed.
4. Hidden costs
Care out of network at in-network cost-sharing, complaints, audits and manual calls. Inferred: we found no plan-level figures.
The common thread: regulators and courts ask what the plan checked, and when. A dated record answers that.
Sources: Ballard Spahr summary of the CAA directory rules; California AG; Becker’s; Pollock Cohen. Not legal advice.
WHAT EXISTS TODAY
Today’s fixes are slow and treat every listing the same
What exists
What it does, with figures
The gap
Provider self-attestation (CAQH)
One large plan: 76% of providers attested in 3 months, 84% accuracy score, 1.2M outreach calls replaced
The provider’s own word; new-patient flag stays unverified
Plan call campaigns and audits
Calls are the best check but costly (CAQH). In secret-shopper calls, 18% got an appointment
Same effort on every listing; slow
Voice AI for insurer calls (SuperDial, Infinitus)
3–8 min vs 24 per call; $3–5 vs $12–14 (vendor-reported, benefits checks)
Not shown for directories; no ranking by dollars
Credentialing automation (Verifiable, Medallion)
Continuous checks of licenses, sanctions and exclusions
Proves who they are, not whether they have room
Honest note: we found no tool that ranks directory checks by dollars at risk. Our search was not exhaustive.
Sources: CAQH case study (2023); Senate Finance Committee; SuperDial and Infinitus pages (vendor claims); Verifiable; Medallion.

HOW WE BUILD IT · ARCHITECTURE
From a screen to a phone call and back to a dashboard
Product names as we understand Microsoft’s current lineup; confirm during build. Health data brings HIPAA duties, so a privacy review comes first.
HOW THE AGENT DECIDES WHO TO CALL FIRST · THE FORMULA
Every listing gets a dollar score
EXPECTED LOSS FOR THE NEXT 90 DAYS
Exposure = P(wrong) × Members who would try it × Cost per failed attempt
P(wrong)
Chance the listing is wrong. Starts as rules: no claims for 6+ months adds risk, a member complaint adds risk, a recent new-patient visit removes risk. Later, a model learns from call results.
Data: claims, complaints, last verified date
Members who would try it
How many members are likely to use this listing in 90 days: recent directory clicks, scaled for local demand (members nearby × how often they seek this specialty).
Data: directory click log, member zip codes
Cost per failed attempt
What it costs the plan when a member hits a ghost: out-of-network care at in-network rates, an ER visit instead of outpatient care, a complaint that becomes a fine.
Data: claim costs, penalty schedule (finance sets it)
All thresholds are starting guesses. Real values come from the plan’s finance and compliance teams.

What one verification call looks like

COST COMPARISON · AN ILLUSTRATIVE MODEL
Checking fewer listings, at lower cost per call
Assume a plan with 50,000 listings, each verified every quarter: 200,000 checks a year.
Staff call every listing
200,000 calls × about $13
$2.6M
AI calls every listing
200,000 calls × about $4
$0.8M
Ours: claims first, then ranked calls
80,000 calls × about $4, if claims clear 60%
$0.32M
$2.28M saved (88%) against staff calls
$0.48M saved (60%) against AI calls to everyone
Per-call costs are SuperDial’s vendor-reported figures for insurer benefits calls, used as a proxy. The 60% is an assumption. Not counted: fines avoided, exposure removed.
WHO WOULD BUY THIS
Plans first, with employers and partners as ways in
Buyers
  • Commercial health plans
  • Medicare Advantage plans, whose directories CMS reviews
  • Medicaid managed-care plans, under OIG scrutiny
  • Behavioral-health administrators
  • State agencies that oversee networks
Your current clients
None is a health plan. The closest route in is employers that sponsor health plans, such as J&J, Ardent Mills and UNFI.
Check which self-fund and who administers the plan. The suits against Carelon and EmblemHealth were brought by public-employer plan members.
Partners and channels
  • Third-party administrators
  • Credentialing vendors, whose license and sanction flags feed our checks
  • Microsoft health and life sciences co-sell
  • Dental and vision plans
Best first target: a plan already under scrutiny for behavioral-health access, where the cost of doing nothing is visible.
Employer-plan scope of the directory rules to be confirmed by a compliance review. Client names from the team’s own list.
GO-TO-MARKET
Prove it beside the current process, then expand
1 · PROVE · 0–3 MO
Shadow pilot with one plan, one state, mental-health listings. Change nothing in the live directory. Measure exposure removed per call.
2 · LAND · 3–9 MO
Go live for that plan. Add Agent 2 claim flags. Test pricing: per verified listing, or a share of exposure removed.
3 · EXPAND · 9–18 MO
More specialties and lines (Medicare Advantage, Medicaid). Add administrators. List on Microsoft’s marketplace and co-sell.
4 · PLATFORM
Apply the same engine to other lists that go stale, as on the next slide.
To compliance: dated evidence of every check
To finance: dollars of risk removed per call
To network teams: fewer calls, fewer complaints
Retire these risks first: offices hanging up on automated calls, whether regulators accept claims as verification, and the privacy review.
Timings and pricing models are proposals to test, not commitments.
FUTURE SCOPE
Not just mental health: any list that goes stale
Three tests: the list drives money. It goes out of date. A call or a web check can verify it.
Next, in health insurance
  • All specialties. OIG found errors for maternal health, and a Pennsylvania study found them across seven specialties
  • Medicare Advantage and Medicaid lines
  • Dental and vision plans
Other industries, to validate
  • Supplier and vendor details behind payments
  • Workers’ compensation provider panels
  • Auto repair-shop networks
  • Store hours and stock listings in retail
Product path: a “verified on [date]” badge for members, then member feedback that re-queues listings the same day.
Sources: HHS-OIG (2026); American Journal of Managed Care (2024). Other industries are ideas we have not yet researched.
